title: Law and justice
note: A criminal case runs in order: a grand jury may indict (formally charge), the court arraigns (calls the accused to plead), and the jury convicts or acquits. Proscribe means forbid; do not confuse it with prescribe, to order or direct. De facto means in fact, whatever the law says; de jure means by law.

read.title: The Case of the Missing Paintings
text: When four paintings vanished from a small museum, suspicion fell on a night guard. A grand jury indicted him for theft, and at his arraignment he pleaded not guilty. The prosecution's case rested on an affidavit from a second guard, who swore she had seen him carrying a large package to his car.

Then the defense subpoenaed the museum's phone records. They showed that the second guard had been talking to an art dealer for weeks. Under questioning she admitted that the dealer had offered her money to blame her colleague. It was a clear attempt to suborn testimony, and the affidavit itself was perjury.

The jury acquitted the first guard, and a later investigation exonerated him completely. The dealer and the second guard, it emerged, had planned the theft in collusion, and both were charged. The paintings were recovered from a storage unit, and the court ordered restitution to the museum for the cost of the search.

The judge who had handled early hearings recused himself from the second trial; he had once bought a print from the dealer. No one was allowed to act with impunity, and the case shows why courts test sworn statements rather than simply accept them.

q.q: Why was the second guard's affidavit perjury?
o: It was a false statement made under oath
It was written by the dealer

q.q: What is the difference between the acquittal and the exoneration?
o: The jury found him not guilty; the investigation cleared him completely
The exoneration was overturned on appeal

q.q: Why did the judge recuse himself?
o: He had a connection to the dealer that suggested possible bias
The guard asked for a jury
